stories.title: Nvidia’s $3.5B MediaTek bet reveals its plan for tackling Big Tech’s AI chip buildout
stories.summary: Nvidia invests $3.5 billion into Taiwanese chipmaker MediaTek. The deal shows how Nvidia plans to stay essential to AI infrastructure as Big Tech begins to build its own AI chips.

sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: Nvidia’s $3.5B MediaTek bet reveals its plan for tackling Big Tech’s AI chip buildout
sources.text: Nvidia is investing $3.5 billion into Taiwanese chipmaker MediaTek. As part of the deal, MediaTek will adopt Nvidia’s technology that will help it design custom chips for AI companies and hyperscalers that can be plugged directly into Nvidia-based data centers. The deal comes as a growing number of AI companies and major cloud providers like Amazon, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic invest in building their own chips so they can be less reliant on Nvidia’s GPUs. Deals like this one with MediaTek allow Nvidia to cede ground to custom silicon while still maintaining its lead as the dominant data center scaffolding. “Nvidia is an AI infrastructure company,” Dion Harris, Nvidia’s senior director of HPC and AI hyperscaler infrastructure solutions, said on Monday on a call with reporters. “We expanded beyond pure computing chips years ago.” The partnership underscores the circular nature of Nvidia’s financing efforts over the past few years, which have often seen the chip giant investing in companies that flow back into its own ecosystem. The deal will give MediaTek access to Nvidia’s NVLink Fusion ecosystem, including NVLink, the technology that lets any chips — even if they’re not Nvidia’s chips — communicate with each other quickly. Last week, Nvidia announced a similar partnership with Amazon Web Services, albeit without the direct investment. AWS will deploy an additional 2 million Nvidia GPUs across its infrastructure, and also integrate NVLink Fusion. With the Nvidia partnership, MediaTek can continue to build custom chips designed by cloud companies or AI labs tailored to their workloads, leveraging Nvidia’s “proven scale-up and scale-out technology stack and ecosystem” and “rack-scale architecture.” “Basically, every cloud, every model builder is deploying our platform in some shape, form, or fashion,” Harris said. “So by MediaTek being able to offer this extension to its customers, it allows them to standardize on the rack-scale infrastructure across their AI factories… and also deploy their [custom chips] right alongside those using the same standard platform.” “This is really about opening up this ecosystem to the entire MediaTek customer base,” Harris continued. MediaTek hasn’t publicly shared information about its customer base as it relates to custom AI chips, but it’s clear Nvidia aims to help it boost that side of the business so long as it can come along for the ride. MediaTek has been slowly building its custom data center ASIC (application-specific integrated circuit) operations, saying in June that it expects the business to generate $2 billion in revenue in 2026, and hopes to target more of the market in the coming years. Given MediaTek’s expertise in developing custom chips that power smartphones , smart homes, automobiles, and wireless communications, the company will also continue to collaborate with Nvidia on DGX Spark, the company’s small developer-focused desktop AI computer. The companies have extended their collaboration with the RTX Spark, Nvidia’s push to put its AI tech into consumer AI PCs. MediaTek and Nvidia will also continue “developing platforms for AI-powered, software-defined vehicles in the era of physical AI,” per a press release. MediaTek’s auto platforms rely on Nvidia’s RTX graphics for intelligent vehicle cockpits and work alongside Nvidia Drive AGX, the company’s in-car computing platform for autonomous driving workloads. “AI is transforming every computing platform — from the world’s largest AI factories to the PC and the car,” Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of Nvidia, said in a statement. “Together, we’re building platforms that bring NVIDIA accelerated computing to new markets and give customers the freedom to create differentiated AI systems at enormous scale.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . sources.name: SiliconANGLE
sources.title: Nvidia invests $3.5B in MediaTek as part of expanded AI chip partnership
sources.text: Nvidia Corp. has bought $3.5 billion worth of MediaTek Inc. convertible bonds as part of an expanded partnership that the companies announced today. A convertible bond is a debt instrument that the buyer can turn into shares later on. Nvidia regularly buys stakes in partners as part of technical collaborations. Earlier this year, it purchased $2 billion worth of shares in Marvell Technologies Inc., a MediaTek competitor. Taiwan-based MediaTek is best known as a supplier of smartphone and connected device processors. It also has a custom chip design business that specializes in artificial intelligence accelerators. According to Nvidia, that unit is the first focus of the newly expanded partnership. Companies that hire MediaTek to design an AI accelerator can choose from a catalog of on-chip networking technologies. Some can connect the processor to other chips in the same rack, while others facilitate data movement across racks. Going forward, MediaTek will offer Nvidia’s NVLink Fusion networking technology as an interconnect option. AI racks contain not only graphics processing units but also central processing units that perform supporting tasks such as organizing the data processed by AI models. NVLink Fusion enables Nvidia’s GPUs and CPUs to exchange data with third-party GPUs and CPUs, respectively. One of technology’s main selling points is its speed. NVLink, the interconnect that underpins NVLink Fusion, can move data more than 10 times faster than a standard implementation of PCIe 6.0. Last week, Nvidia upgraded the technology by adding support for a new memory design approach called NVHBM. The onboard HBM memory in which graphics cards store data is managed by a tiny chip called a memory controller. NVHBM moves the controller from the GPU’s logic die to the die that contains the HBM memory. According to Nvidia, that change boosts data movement speeds while lowering power consumption. The second focus of the company’s expanded MediaTek partnership is the personal computing market. In 2025, Nvidia launched a workstation called the DGX Spark that developers can use for tasks such as fine-tuning AI models. It’s powered by a system-on-chip that MediaTek helped design. The two companies subsequently collaborated on the RTX Spark, a laptop and desktop processor that debuted in June. Nvidia stated today that it plans to collaborate with MediaTek on multiple future generations of the RTX Spark and DGX Spark. The latter company’s exact role was not detailed. However, the current-generation RTX Spark and DGX Spark chips might offer clues. MediaTek helped develop the chips’ onboard CPUs along with certain other components such as the RTX Spark’s memory controller. The companies’ expanded partnership also prioritizes the auto sector. MediaTek sells a series of systems-on-chip called Dimensity Auto that carmakers use to power in-vehicle displays. The processors include, among others, an Nvidia graphics rendering chiplet. The companies stated today they plan to continue working together on software-defined vehicle chips. “Together, we’re building platforms that bring Nvidia accelerated computing to new markets and give customers the freedom to create differentiated AI systems at enormous scale,” said Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang. MediaTek, for its part, is strengthening a partnership that supports one of its fastest-growing businesses. The company recently doubled its full-year revenue forecast for its data center chip design group to $2 billion. It hopes to grow that number severalfold in the coming years. stories.title: OpenAI's ad business shows blistering growth, hits $1 billion annualized revenue run rate
stories.summary: OpenAI's move to serve ads in ChatGPT earlier this year drew ridicule from its chief rival, Anthropic, in the form of a Super Bowl commercial.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: OpenAI's ad business shows blistering growth, hits $1 billion annualized revenue run rate
sources.text: OpenAI on Monday announced that its advertising business has hit $1 billion in annualized revenue run rate, a milestone that the company is touting as proof of its "diversified business model." The artificial intelligence company is gearing up for what is expected to be a massive initial public offering , and is under pressure to justify its $852 billion valuation to investors. OpenAI said Monday that its ad business, which is roughly 200 days old, builds on its existing revenue engines like its enterprise offerings, consumer subscriptions and usage-based application programming interfaces. OpenAI began testing ads within its ChatGPT chatbot in the U.S. in February, a decision that was both highly anticipated and controversial. Digital advertising has long been the cash cow for other big tech companies like Google and Meta , but OpenAI's move was ridiculed by its chief rival, Anthropic , which made OpenAI's ad push the focus of its first Super Bowl campaign . ChatGPT Ads are now available in more than 40 countries, and OpenAI said it's rolling out self-service access across India, Europe, the Middle East and North Africa on Monday. Ads within the chatbot appear for OpenAI's Go subscribers and its free tier, which makes up the vast majority of its 1 billion weekly active users. OpenAI said Monday that its ads are clearly labeled and do not influence ChatGPT's answers. Advertisers do not have access to users' private conversations. "Our next phase of growth will bring ChatGPT Ads to more markets and introduce additional formats, objectives, buying options, and measurement capabilities," OpenAI said in a release. "We will also explore new ways for businesses to interact with consumers in more native ways in ChatGPT." — CNBC's Kate Rooney contributed to this report. WATCH: Experts weigh in on the market’s ability to handle Anthropic and OpenAI going public

sources.name: SiliconANGLE
sources.title: OpenAI says its ad business has already hit $1B in annualized revenue
sources.text: OpenAI Group PBC today sought to justify its controversial decision to start running ads in ChatGPT several months ago, saying its new advertising business has now crossed the $1 billion annualized revenue run rate mark. In a blog post , OpenAI said the milestone underlines its success in creating a “diversified business model” that gives people more choice about how to access its products, alongside its consumer subscriptions, enterprise offerings and its application programming interfaces. The announcement comes at a time when OpenAI is facing increased pressure to justify an $852 billion valuation ahead of what’s expected to be a massive initial public offering that could launch later this year. But the new ad business , which launched around 200 days ago, is still responsible for only a small part of the company’s total revenue. Last month, it was reported that the company generated $6.7 billion in second quarter sales, up 18% from the first quarter. Those numbers were viewed as disappointing, as just a day earlier OpenAI’s rival Anthropic PBC reported that its own revenue had grown more than 50%, to $11.6 billion, over the same period, also posting a small profit. OpenAI, in contrast, saw its operating loss grow to $12.3 billion. Still, OpenAI tried to give prospective investors reason to be optimistic that the ad business can help it turn things around. It said it’s aiming to accelerate growth, with a target of $2.5 billion in ad revenue by the end of the year and is tracking toward total annualized revenue exceeding $40 billion. OpenAI started testing ads within ChatGPT in February with a small number of users in the U.S., and has scaled up the experiment rapidly since then. The decision was controversial at the time, but also not unexpected, given that the company’s challenging finances have been public knowledge for a while. Digital ads have proven to be a goldmine for technology giants like Google LLC, Meta Platforms Inc. and Amazon.com Inc. for years, but OpenAI’s decision to go down that road was criticized by Anthropic, which launched a series of Super Bowl ads ridiculing its rival. But OpenAI has been undeterred, and in today’s announcement it revealed that it’s now expanding ads in ChatGPT to more than 40 new countries, including India and others across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. The ads appear for ChatGPT Go subscribers and free-tier users directly within the model’s responses to questions and prompts. Those users make up the vast majority of its 1 billion active weekly users. The company said it has established ad partnerships with more than 50 brands via agencies such as Omnicom and WPP, and it made an effort to entice even more to consider using ChatGPT for outreach. In its blog post, it related a couple of success stories, saying that one e-commerce brand was able to achieve a three-fold return on its ad spending across multiple campaigns in just 28 days. Another technology partner reported that more than 80% of its ChatGPT traffic came from new customers. The company reiterated once more that its ads are all clearly labeled and do not have any influence on ChatGPT’s outputs. Advertisers do not have access to user’s private conversations with ChatGPT. Besides bringing ads to more markets, OpenAI said it’s going to experiment with new ad formats, buying options and measurement capabilities, so that businesses will be able to interact with consumers in more “native ways” within ChatGPT. stories.title: ChatGPT atinge receita anual de US$ 1 bilhão com anúncios
stories.summary: Valor foi alcançado em apenas seis meses desde o início da disponibilização. Atualmente, disponível em torno de 40 países, a ferramenta deve chegar a novos destinos, segundo a OpenAI

sources.name: Mobile Time
sources.title: ChatGPT atinge receita anual de US$ 1 bilhão com anúncios
sources.text: A renda anual do ChatGPT ( Android , iOS ) com anúncios atingiu a marca de US$ 1 bilhão. O serviço, chamado de ChatGPT Ads, foi disponibilizado em fevereiro deste ano , com a premissa de não misturar publicidade com as respostas do modelo. Ele está disponível em cerca de 40 países, inclusive no Brasil, mas o número deve crescer, segundo a OpenAI . De acordo com a companhia, a plataforma soma dezenas de milhares de anunciantes. Um deles, conseguiu um retorno três vezes maior do que o investido na publicidade, em apenas 28 dias de campanha. Outro disse que em torno de 80% do tráfego de novos usuários vem da IA. No anúncio, a big tech também comunicou a disponibilidade de autoatendimento para adquirir publicidade no ChatGPT, através do seu gerenciador. Por ora, esse caminho só pode ser utilizado por usuários de África, Índia, Europa e Ásia Ocidental. A OpenAI pretende expandir. sources.name: Tecmundo
sources.title: Anúncios do ChatGPT devem render US$ 1 bilhão para a OpenAI em 2026
sources.text: Anúncios do ChatGPT devem render US$ 1 bilhão para a OpenAI em 2026 Empresa comemora marco de nova forma de receita, amplia alcance do programa e estuda novos formatos de publicidade na plataforma. A empresa de inteligência artificial (IA) OpenAI está satisfeita com a inserção de anúncios no ChatGPT . De acordo com um comunicado oficial nesta segunda-feira (31), a previsão é de que essa fonte já renda US$ 1 bilhão (mais de R$ 5,1 bilhões) para os cofres da companhia . O valor foi obtido a partir da taxa de receita anualizada , ou seja, uma projeção matemática do rendimento para 12 meses com base no que foi arrecadado até agora. A ideia é que, caso mais anunciantes estejam interessados e a taxa de usuários também aumente, esse número seja ainda maior. Os anúncios do ChatGPT começaram a rodar oficialmente apenas há cerca de 200 dias. Eles foram especulados a partir do fim de 2025, quando a OpenAI passou a se preocupar mais com a demora para gerar receita e a perspectiva tardia de obtenção de lucro. Após um mês de teste , a exibição oficial de anúncios começou em fevereiro deste ano em alguns mercados, em um espaço ao fim da resposta da IA que deixa evidente que aquele é um conteúdo patrocinado. Usuários brasileiros começaram a ver anúncios no ChatGPT a partir do início de outubro . Ainda assim, foram muitas as críticas sobre a adição de anúncios na ferramenta , inclusive do ponto de vista de privacidade e riscos de interesses comerciais interferirem nas entregas da plataforma — todas defendidas pela OpenAI, que alega que a experiencia seguirá a mesma. stories.title: Trump says U.S. communities opposing AI data centers could end up 'backwards and poor'
stories.summary: "China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement," Trump said as Republicans express concerns about the backlash to data centers.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Trump says U.S. communities opposing AI data centers could end up 'backwards and poor'
sources.text: President Donald Trump on Monday blasted communities that oppose new data centers as Republicans confront voter backlash over the projects ahead of November's midterm elections . "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. "If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign," the president said. "The good news is that there are plenty of other places that want them. If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame. China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement. Actually, they can't believe it is happening!" Trump's post comes nearly a week after a memo issued by the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned, "If voters' perceptions of data centers are not fixed quickly, the campaign against them will expand far beyond Ohio." The NRSC said that private polling in that state shows Republican Sen. Jon Husted in a "dead heat" with Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown in the special election to fill the remainder of the term for the seat vacated by Vice President JD Vance. In May, Gallup said a survey conducted in March found that "seven in 10 Americans oppose constructing data centers for artificial intelligence in their local area, including nearly half, 48%, who are strongly opposed." On Aug. 28, Wolfe Research issued a report that said, "In nearly every meeting with investors over the past month or so, we've been asked: How is the voter backlash against data centers going to play out?" "The pace and scale of the backlash is genuinely breathtaking — we've never seen anything like it," the report said. "We've seen 60-point drops in net support for local data center (DC) construction across party lines over the past 12 months." The upcoming midterm elections will determine which party controls both chambers of Congress. Republicans hold a narrow majority in the House of Representatives, and a 53-47 majority in the Senate. AI data centers house computing equipment used to train and operate artificial intelligence models developed by companies including OpenAI and Anthropic . The rush to build data centers has sparked a backlash in communities across the U.S., with opponents raising concerns about electricity costs, power demand, water use and other local impacts. In its Aug. 18 memo, the NRSC warned that "the current perception is negative" among Americans about data centers as it detailed how the issue is affecting the race for the Senate in Ohio. "Private polling has been consistent: when voters hear Brown's positions and his record, Husted pulls away. That is still the path in this race," the memo said. "The new ingredient (and the new problem) is data centers. "Ohio is one of the leaders in building these AI factories," the NRSC said. "Brown has made his opposition to them the centerpiece of his campaign against Husted. Brown is using it because it works." "More than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted's neck. If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one."

sources.name: TechRadar
sources.title: 'Let data reign'; Trump warns that those who don't let AI data centers proliferate will end up 'backwards and poor'
sources.text: AI has supercharged data center growth and sparked power, resource, and noise concerns, turning it into one massive hot-button topic for consumers The growth and expansion of generative AI is unprecedented, surpassed only, perhaps, by the rapid expansion and impact of the data centers that support it. While anti-data center sentiment is on the rise , US President Donald Trump took to his Truth Social social media platform on Monday to urge people to support rapid data center growth, warning those who oppose that "the only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is that they want to end up being backwards and poor." Before we dive into the rest of Trump's post, it's worth stepping back to look at data center construction growth and the more recent and somewhat remarkable backlash. Data centers are not just an artificial intelligence phenomenon. These large buildings packed with servers and connected to the Internet have been around for decades and initially marked their greatest expansion during the rise of the World Wide Web. As the Internet grew in the 1990s and the number of websites skyrocketed, data centers that could keep copies of these sites and their data and then serve them to whoever wanted to access them around the world popped up around the world. Modern-day cloud systems like Amazon Web Services (AWS) serve millions of websites with a reported 900 data centers . The recent rapid rise of AI usage around the globe in the form of ChatGPT , Claude , and Gemini has supercharged a new kind of data center growth. While traditional cloud servers relied on relatively efficient CPUs, generative AI demands more powerful and power-hungry GPUs, primarily from Nvidia . According to the World Resources Institute, a single AI data center can eat as much energy as 100,000 homes . When you consume that kind of energy, you also generate a lot of heat, and one of the other earmarks of modern AI data centers is their use of water for cooling. The WRI reports that a large AI data center can consume up to 5 million gallons of water a day. Finally, these large data centers can be loud, producing a constant hum that can be heard in nearby communities. These issues are being amplified by the stunning growth of these data centers. Cleanview reports roughly 3,400 US data centers , with another 2,059 planned. Many of these massive buildings are planned along the eastern seaboard of the US and in Texas, where the governor recently instituted a moratorium . Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more. Perhaps more concerning are the AI data centers planned for Colorado, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, and New Mexico, where a lengthy drought and the shrinking Colorado River are leading to water shortages that may result in far more stringent water conservation measures. It's unclear how AI data center plans sync with that. In the meantime, public opinion on data centers has shifted. A May 2026 Gallup poll found that 7 in 10 Americans oppose local construction of AI data centers , basically a "not in my town" sentiment. As expected, chief concerns revolve around the environment and quality of life. Many are also worried about resources. In the midst of all this, we have the US leadership trying to encourage people to just let AI data center companies build. Here's Trump's full post: "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is that they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign. The good news is that there are plenty of other places that want them. If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame. China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement. Actually, they can't believe it is happening!" Trump is right that data centers can result in an economic boom, including investment and new jobs, but it can also be short-lived after construction is done. Basically, the workforce is needed for the build and setup, and t hen automation tends to take on the majority of the day-to-day workload . The concern about falling behind China in the AI race is more supportable in that there is undoubtedly an AI global supremacy race. With its lack of regulation and fewer open-source models, the US has not necessarily done itself any favors. And it's safe to assume that Chinese citizens have little say in the power, resources, and quality-of-life impacts of AI data center development and construction. Still, the idea that consumers, as opposed to AI companies, and the companies that build, support, and invest in these companies, will get rich is — well — rich. Communities can potentially benefit economically if the tax base is spread over these massive structures (utilities in your town can have a similar effect), therefore taking some of the burden off residents, but that doesn't address water, electricity, sound, and aesthetic concerns. Some data center developers are working with communities and local utilities to ensure they pay their fair share of electricity (and maybe manage electricity use) and reuse water, but no regulation ensures these data centers are built responsibly. Naturally, Trump does not address any of those worries in his post, and his administration has in recent days worked with the EPA to try and remove opportunities for communities to comment on the construction of these AI data centers before they're built in their communities. "Let data reign" sounds like a campaign slogan that might work for more simplistic issues, but Trump's promises of jobs and wealth for all are likely to fall flat with communities who see the cranes dotting the landscape, walls rising from the dust and, eventually, resources being sucked dry.
